author: EmuCore - Hub
title: PCSX2 enters its Qt interface era
summary: The Qt migration rebuilt PCSX2's desktop experience around a consistent, cross-platform interface rather than the limitations of the former wxWidgets front end.
heroAlt: PCSX2 enters its Qt interface era
searchKeywords: PCSX2 enters its Qt interface era

blocks.text: Before the 2.0 generation, PCSX2's wxWidgets front end was not cleanly separated from emulation work. The project documents deadlocks and race conditions caused by that coupling, while years of accumulated menus made ordinary configuration difficult to follow. Replacing the toolkit was therefore an architecture change: the emulator needed a desktop shell that could observe VM state without becoming part of the timing-sensitive VM itself.
A desktop interface rebuilt in Qt

The new front end was led by Stenzek, drawing on experience from DuckStation's Qt application. PCSX2 did not wrap the old dialogs in a new theme; settings pages, library views and state handling were rebuilt around Qt. The result is one maintained desktop interface for Windows, Linux and macOS, with shared behavior instead of three increasingly different sets of platform widgets.
The game library becomes the starting point

Qt's grid and list views put the scanned game library at the center of the desktop workflow. A user can open global settings, a title's properties or a boot action from the same library context. Themes and scalable widgets improve presentation, but the important change is navigational: game-specific choices no longer live in plug-in dialogs that forget which title the user is trying to configure.
Clear boundary with the fullscreen interface

PCSX2's controller-first Big Picture experience uses its own ImGui-based fullscreen UI; it is not simply the Qt window enlarged for a television. Both interfaces operate on the same emulator configuration and game data. That boundary lets the desktop UI remain efficient for keyboard-and-mouse diagnostics while the fullscreen path uses large controller targets, without duplicating the underlying settings model.
Why the migration enabled later work

Removing the old GUI/core entanglement made per-game settings, automatic GameDB fixes and cross-platform maintenance easier to integrate into one release process. A UI bug can now be investigated in the Qt layer without treating it as an emulation-core timing change. The official 2.0 retrospective and the maintained `pcsx2-qt` source tree provide complementary evidence: one explains the design decision, while the other shows the interface as an active part of the project. The maintained source layout reinforces that separation: desktop presentation lives under the Qt front-end code while VM, settings and game-list services remain reusable. This lets accessibility, scaling and navigation work advance without forking emulator behavior, and it gives Linux, macOS and Windows users the same settings vocabulary when they compare a problem or follow project documentation.
